A persistent characteristic of 2025 SCS outbreaks has been 
instances of torrential rainfall spawning flash flooding. These SCS 
driven flash-flooding events were aided by multiple factors, which 
included cut-off (stuck) low pressure systems in tandem with 
persistent flow from the Gulf and / or training (repeating) storms 
that formed near urban regions or recent burn scars. Notable 
events included flash flooding in the Texas Hill Country, Ruidoso 
(New Mexico), New York City (New York), Chicago (Illinois), and 
Milwaukee (Wisconsin) among others. In many instances, low 
National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) take up rates meant 
most of the flood-related damage went uninsured.
United States
SCS losses in the US continued to drive a substantial portion 
of global insured SCS losses during the first nine months of 
2025. Most of the losses were incurred following a highly active 
period for the peril during the peak months between March and 
June. US SCS accounted for 44% of global insured losses alone 
through Q3. To date, the US has experienced 13 billion-dollar 
insured SCS loss events, of which five saw multi-billion-dollar 
industry loss totals (USD2+ billion). 
2025 marked the third consecutive year in which US SCS insured 
losses through September exceeded USD40 billion. When 
extending to the full calendar year, 2025 already ranks as the 
fourth-costliest year for insurers on record – only behind 2023 
(USD62 billion), 2024 (USD57 billion), and 2020 (USD47 billion). 
As some of the larger 2025 outbreaks continue to be assessed 
and claims are processed, further loss progression is expected in 
the months ahead.
